difficultyRationale: Choosing between the two common List implementations by access pattern is a foundational Java collections recognition task.
prompt: A service builds a report by appending rows one at a time, then repeatedly looks up rows by numeric index (`get(i)`) to render a table, with no insertions or removals in the middle of the list. Which `List` implementation fits this access pattern best, and why?
explanation: `ArrayList` backs its elements with a resizable array, so `get(i)` is a direct, constant-time index into that array. `LinkedList` has to walk node-to-node from one end to reach index `i`, which costs time proportional to `i`'s distance from the nearer end. Since this workload appends at the end and then does many indexed reads, with no middle insertions or removals, `ArrayList` is the better fit.

options.text: `LinkedList`, because it never needs to resize an internal array the way `ArrayList` does when it grows.
options.explanation: True but irrelevant here: occasional array growth is amortized and cheap, while `LinkedList`'s per-access traversal cost for repeated indexed reads is the larger cost in this workload.

options.text: `ArrayList`, because indexed `get` is a constant-time array access, while `LinkedList` must traverse nodes from one end to reach the index.
options.explanation: Correct: `ArrayList.get(i)` reads the backing array directly, independent of list size, while `LinkedList.get(i)` walks the node chain, which is linear in the distance to the index — exactly the cost this read-heavy, index-based workload would pay repeatedly.

options.text: `LinkedList`, because appending to the end of an `ArrayList` is not supported without first converting it to an array.
options.explanation: Incorrect premise: `ArrayList.add` appends in amortized constant time with no conversion step; nothing about appending favors `LinkedList` here.

options.text: Either works identically, since both implement the same `List` interface and therefore offer the same performance characteristics for any operation.
options.explanation: Implementing the same interface guarantees the same operations are available, not the same cost; `List`'s contract says nothing about the time complexity each implementation must deliver.
